To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Holy Land, as it was perceived by the Western world in the course of nineteenth and twentieth century, was not the result an objective description of Palestine and its people; on the contrary it was the result of a narrative carefully constructed to fit the narrators’ purpose.
the invention of the “primitive society” was a narrative carefully designed and constructed to serve the interests of its inventors.
the Western perception of “Palestine as a primitive land” has been a major factor in shaping the intellectual and political discourse about the Holy Land.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the intellectual origins of the Palestine– Israel conflict.

the question of how Western perceptions of the Holy Land were shaped in the course of time, how they were used and how these perceptions influenced the political and religious debates about the future of the land.
the intellectual origins of the Palestine-Israel conflict.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the invention of the primitive Palestinian society was an important step in the making of Palestine as a land for the Jews.
the “primitive Palestine” of the Western imagination was a construct, not a reflection of reality.
the “primitive society” narrative, as a product of the Western imagination, was not a mere reflection of the “realities” on the ground.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated how the invention of primitive society was used as a tool to justify the colonization of Palestine and the creation of the state of Israel.
the invention of primitive Palestine was a key factor in the making of the Palestine–Israeli conflict.
the Western view of Palestine was a product of Western interests and that this view was shaped by Western perceptions of the Orient, and in particular by the idea of a “primitive society”.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way we look at the world and its peoples is a reflection of our own cultural and political preconceptions and prejudices.
the way the West viewed and still views Palestine is a narrative that was created in the course of history and is therefore subject to change.
the way the Western public and the international community looked at the land of Palestine and its people was shaped and determined by Western intellectual and political agendas.
